parse.src: A stylised near-field to biosphere chain: a repository inventory leaks into the geosphere, which discharges to a soil layer, which is leached into a well used for drinking water. Dose is the well concentration times an ingestion rate and a dose coefficient. Illustrative parameter values only. Most parameters carry a distribution, so the model can be run probabilistically; the ICRP dose coefficients are deliberately left fixed.
Release from the waste form, nuclide specific
Sorption in the soil layer; retards leaching
Bulk density of the solid, in the retardation factor.
Water-filled porosity, in the retardation factor.

Move the controls to see what each does to the dose from the well, and run the spread to see how uncertain it is at those values. The model itself is not changed: every run is of a copy at the values the controls hold.
Dose to somebody drinking from the well

The inventory of each compartment, in becquerels, as the release works its way down the chain: out of the **repository**, through the **geosphere** and the **soil**, and into the **well**. The other tab has the dose in numbers.

The controls are on the first page. Every page reads the same run, so what they do shows here too.

A ball thrown straight up from the floor at 20 m/s, falling back under gravity and bouncing with 0.9 of the speed it landed with: the classic test of how a solver handles events. Height is the one compartment. Bounce is a trigger that fires when Height falls through zero, so the solver stops exactly there and starts again. Each bounce takes two snapshots, its time (T_bounce) and the speed the ball leaves the floor with (V_up), and between bounces the ball's Velocity is V_up − g·(t − T_bounce).

The landing speed is read off the flight time: a flight from the floor and back takes 2V/g, so the ball lands at g times half its time in the air. That keeps V_up from reading its own value, which a snapshot may not do. The bounces come where the closed form (2·v0/g)·(1 − eⁿ)/(1 − e) puts them: 4.08, 7.75 and 11.05 s, and so on, twelve in the thirty seconds, with the energy falling to e² = 0.81 of itself at each.

Try: run it to 45 s. The bounces pile up towards (2·v0/g)/(1 − e) = 40.8 s, where infinitely many of them would happen in a finite time (Zeno behaviour). After about a hundred, the flights are too short to resolve and the ball falls through the floor. That is a property of the model, which needs a rule for coming to rest, not a fault in the solver.

Prigogine and Lefever's model of an autocatalytic reaction, the Brusselator. A feeds X; X turns into Y at rate B·X; two X and a Y make three X, at rate X²·Y; and X leaves at rate X. With A and B held at 1 and 3, each of those steps is a source or a transfer on the diagram, and together they make dX/dt = A + X²Y − (B + 1)X and dY/dt = BX − X²Y.

The steady state (A, B/A) = (1, 3) is unstable whenever B > 1 + A², so instead of settling the concentrations run round a limit cycle, X spiking every 7.15 seconds.

Try: B = 1.5. Below the threshold the oscillations die away, into the steady state (1, 1.5).

A single compartment holding pure Pu-241, showing ingrowth down the 4n+1 chain: Pu-241 to Am-241 to Np-237 to U-233 to Th-229. Nothing moves between compartments here; every feature on the chart comes from the decay and ingrowth terms. The inventories are activities, so a daughter grows in at its own decay constant: Am-241 lives 30 times longer than the Pu-241 feeding it and its activity peaks 34 times lower. Set decay_unit to mol to count atoms instead, and the same run conserves the chain down it.

The linear test equation dy/dt = −k·y with y(0) = y0, whose solution y0·e^(−k·t) is known exactly. It is the equation solvers are designed and analysed on (Dahlquist's test equation), and here it is the smallest compartment model there is: one compartment emptied by a first-order transfer out of the model. Exact is the closed form, worked out at every saved time, so the solver's error can be read straight off the Table: with dp45 at a relative tolerance of 1e-6, y and Exact agree to within 3e-6 after ten time constants. That global error is a little larger than the tolerance, which bounds the error of each step, not of the whole run.

The value axis is logarithmic, so the decay is a straight line.

Try: set k to 1e6. The answer is gone within a few tens of microseconds, yet dp45 still needs three million steps to cross the ten seconds, because an explicit method's step must stay below about 3.3/k to be stable, however accurate a longer one would be. The NDF solver, built for stiff problems, needs 248 steps. That gap is what stiffness means.

A waste vault leaks into a fracture in the host rock; the nuclides travel along it by advection, sorb on the fracture coating and diffuse into the pore water of the rock matrix beside it, and what survives the journey reaches a well. The rock is one FARFCOMP block — a dual-porosity transport model ported from SKB's own farf_comp, with 20 fracture cells and 20 matrix layers per nuclide behind it, and the rock going on past the point the release is measured, as in FARF31 — and the whole thing is solved as one system with the two compartments.

The three nuclides are a decay chain, and they decay and grow into one another everywhere: in the vault, in every cell of the fracture, in every layer of the rock, and in the well. Th-230 hardly reaches the well as itself; almost all of what arrives grew in on the way.

Try: the travel time TW and the flow resistance F are what a hydrogeological model supplies, so change them and watch the arrival move. Turn on "Report every cell" in the block's Discretisation section to chart the profile down the fracture and into the rock.
How fast the vault gives up its inventory to the fracture.
The volume the well draws, which dilutes what arrives.
The water in the well that what arrives mixes into. The flow over it is how often that water is replaced: a thousand times a year, so the well's inventory is a steady state.
Sorption in the rock matrix, per nuclide. Thorium is held far harder than uranium, which is why it arrives so much later.
Effective diffusivity: 1e-12 m2/s in the pore water.
The waste. Only U-238 is emplaced; the other two grow in.
What arrives, before it is drawn off.

SKB's FARFCOMP. TW is the water travel time along the path and F the flow-related transport resistance; the rest is the rock and the chemistry. The first matrix layer is left empty, so it is worked out from the path's own time scales — 3.6 mm here, growing by 1.44 to 12.5 m — and the rock goes on past the release point: five cells of it stand for the rock downstream, and what is in them has been released.
Into the first cell of the fracture.
The flux out of the far end of the path. Its rate is the path itself, so there is nothing to set: the block works it out from its own cells.
The well is flushed: each year its water is replaced well_flow / well_volume times, so its inventory is a steady state rather than an accumulation.
What arrives per year, diluted into the volume the well draws. `Rock` is the release out of the far end of the path.
A four-compartment test model. C1 drains to C2 and C3, C2 feeds C3, and C3 discharges to C4. The Outflow expression is the discharge rate times C3, so the release curve can be read directly.

A mass on a spring, x'' = −ω²·x − 2ζω·x', written as two compartments, the position x and the velocity v, whose dy/dt terms read each other. Both swing through zero, so "cannot go negative" is off on each. With no damping (zeta = 0) the mass swings between x = ±1 once a second for ever, and its energy (v² + ω²x²)/2 never changes. Exact is the closed form, which holds for any damping ratio below 1.

Twenty periods are long enough for a solver's phase error to show. At the same relative tolerance of 1e-8, dp45 ends 1.2e-7 from Exact after 1682 steps, and the seventh-order vern7 ends 1.6e-9 away after 562. The NDF solver, made for stiff decay rather than for oscillation, ends 6e-6 away and has lost 1.2e-5 of the energy: its damping is numerical, not physical.

Try: zeta = 0.1 for a damped oscillator, then switch solvers and compare x with Exact.

parse.src: Four nuclides moving through three landscape objects. Compartments are indexed by Radionuclides x Object, so each box on the diagram is really 12 state variables. Sorption is per nuclide, discharge is per object, and the Wetland sub-set drains only the lake and the mire. The three reductions show the two ways of collapsing a dimension: Inventory adds two blocks index by index, TotalWater sums one block over the nuclides, and PeakObject takes the largest object for each nuclide. Solved with the NDF solver, which handles the stiffness from Pb-210 and Ra-226 in a fraction of the steps the Rosenbrock pair needs.
Sorption: nuclide specific, shared across objects
Water turnover: object specific, shared across nuclides

Every object discharges into the one downstream compartment, so this flux is summed over Object on the way in. That is what sum_extra_indices asks for; without it the model is refused, because a flux whose ends do not correspond is far more often a mistake than an intention.
Only the wetlands lose water this way; the forest does not. Indexed by Radionuclides x Wetland, and the Wetland sub-set resolves onto the Object dimension of the compartments.
Every nuclide in the water of each object -- the sum this used to spell out by hand.
The worst object for each nuclide.
Regolith and water together, object by object.

Two lookup tables drive the model: the groundwater flow through a biosphere object over a glacial cycle, and the lake area as the basin silts up. Both are read at the simulation clock, which is what makes a lookup table a time-dependent parameter rather than a constant. The advective transfer follows Q_gw / V, so its rate -- and the Jacobian -- move with time; the dose expression divides by the lake area, which is what the table is there to say.
Mean depth of the lake: area times this is its volume.
Lake volume, so the groundwater flow becomes a turnover rate.
Groundwater flow through the object. Nearly stops under permafrost, between 9000 and 12000 years.
Lake surface area. The basin silts up: by 16000 years only a small pond is left.

Lorenz's 1963 model of convection, dx/dt = σ(y − x), dy/dt = x(ρ − z) − y and dz/dt = xy − βz, with his σ = 10, ρ = 28 and β = 8/3: the system that made chaos famous. The solution never settles and never repeats. x swings irregularly between −18 and 20 as the state circles one lobe of the butterfly-shaped attractor and then the other, while z rises and falls between about 1 and 48. x and y go negative, so "cannot go negative" is off on all three.

Chaos means that any difference grows about tenfold every two and a half seconds, a solver's own errors included. Run the model with dp45, vern7 and the NDF solver at the same tight tolerance (1e-10): they agree to four figures at t = 20, have parted by t = 28, and by the end are unrelated, with x(50) at 6.32, 4.99 and −0.81. Each is as good an answer as the others to a question whose answer cannot be known that far ahead.

The predator–prey equations of Lotka and Volterra: prey x breed at rate α and are eaten at β·x·y; predators y breed by eating, at δ·x·y, and die at rate γ. Each population's growth is its compartment's dy/dt term, and each reads the other compartment. With α = 1.5, β = 1, γ = 3 and δ = 1, and both populations starting at 1, they cycle round the equilibrium (γ/δ, α/β) = (3, 1.5) every 3.32 years, the predators' peaks trailing the prey's by about half a year.

The cycles neither grow nor fade, because δx − γ·ln x + βy − α·ln y is conserved along every orbit. That is the Invariant expression, which stays within 1e-7 of 2 over the twenty years here. How far it drifts is a direct measure of a solver's error: at the tolerance set here (1e-8) dp45 holds it to 1.4e-7 in 461 steps, while the second-order ros23 needs 6541 steps and drifts by 7e-6. Loosen the tolerance to 1e-4 and the invariant wanders by a few parts in a thousand.

parse.tree: (- (+ (- (* (ref delta) (ref Prey)) (* (ref gamma) (call log (ref Prey)))) (* (ref beta) (ref Predator))) (* (ref alpha) (call log (ref Predator))))

parse.src:
An enzyme E binds its substrate S into a complex C, at rate kf·E·S. The complex either falls apart again (kr·C) or turns the substrate into product P (kcat·C). The compartments follow the substrate, free, bound and made into product, so Binding, Unbinding and Catalysis are transfers between them and S + C + P stays at S0; the free enzyme is the expression E = E0 − C.

With a hundred times more substrate than enzyme, C fills within half a second and then stays in a quasi-steady state. From then on the rate of product formation follows the Michaelis–Menten law Vmax·S/(Km + S), with Km = (kr + kcat)/kf = 1.5 µM and Vmax = kcat·E0 = 0.05 µM/s: Rate and MM_rate agree to within about 1 % from the first second to the fifth minute. Half the substrate is gone after 119 s. The fast start and the slow tail make the problem mildly stiff, which is why it runs on the NDF solver and is drawn on a logarithmic time axis.

The Oregonator, Field and Noyes's three-variable model of the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction, in the scaled form of the stiff test problem OREGO: y1 is bromous acid, y2 bromide and y3 the cerium catalyst, and each is a compartment with its dy/dt term from that problem. The concentrations swing across five decades, y1 from 1 up to 1.2·10⁵ and back in every cycle, so the value axis is logarithmic. At t = 360 the run is within 4·10⁻⁵ of the problem's reference solution (1.000815, 1228.18, 132.055).

The parameters span seven orders of magnitude and the problem is stiff throughout: the NDF solver crosses the 360 seconds in 1654 steps, dp45 in 3.4 million.

A model with no compartments. Nothing is integrated: the release to the biosphere is a measured series, and the concentration, the dose per nuclide and the total dose follow from it directly. Models of this shape are common — 15 of the 71 real projects this was measured against — and they are what the results of a transport calculation are turned into. The blocks are evaluated over the time span in dependency order, with the same clock a solved model would see.
Share of the release that reaches this recipient.
Release to the biosphere, from a transport calculation. Every nuclide shares the shape here; a real model gives each its own.
Every nuclide together — the number an assessment reports.
The nuclide contributing most at each moment.
Peak dose and when it happened

A release pulse passes through a lake and out again. The five blocks that depend on what has already happened are all here: a discrete event fires when the concentration falls back past a limit, a min/max holds the peak dose, a snapshot remembers the year the limit was crossed, a running mean averages the dose from that year on, and a delay reports the dose a century earlier. Nothing here is a function of the state alone -- each one has to be recorded as the solver goes.
The year the dose falls back through the limit on its way down.

Robertson's three reactions, the classic stiff test problem ROBER: A → B at 0.04 per second, B + B → C + B at 3·10⁷, and B + C → A + C at 10⁴. Each reaction is a transfer whose rate reads the concentrations, so the diagram is the reaction scheme and the three compartments always add up to 1 (the Total expression). The intermediate B never exceeds 3.65·10⁻⁵, which it reaches after 4.6 ms; B_x_1e4 is B times 10⁴, the way it is usually plotted beside A and C.

The run covers seventeen decades of time, from a microsecond to 10¹¹ s, with twenty saved times a decade, and it ends within 10⁻⁷ of the published reference solution at t = 40 and at t = 10¹¹. The rate constants differ by nearly nine orders of magnitude, which is stiffness at its plainest: the NDF solver takes 1760 steps, while dp45 stalls before t = 3 and Tsit5 runs out of its ten million steps before t = 5000. The tolerances are tight (rtol 1e-8, abstol 1e-14) because B, and late in the run A, are numbers a looser absolute tolerance cannot see.

The same model under three futures. `Climate` is a scenario index list: one of its indices is live at a time, chosen under Simulation on the left, and every block indexed by it is read at that one. So `Runoff` and `LakeVolume` hold a value per scenario while `Conc` — which reads the volume but is not itself scenario-indexed — is a single quantity. Switch the scenario and the whole model answers differently, where the usual arrangement is one simulation per scenario.
Alternative futures, not an axis of the model: one runs at a time.
How fast the soil drains into the lake.

Kermack and McKendrick's epidemic model: susceptible people S are infected at rate β·S·I/N, and the infected I recover at rate γ, into R, where they stay. Infection and Recovery are ordinary transfers whose rates read the compartments, so the diagram is the model and S + I + R stays at N = 1000. With β = 0.3 and γ = 0.1 a day, the basic reproduction number R0 = β/γ is 3. One case starts it; the epidemic peaks around day 38 with 301 people infected at once, exactly when S has fallen to N/R0 and R_eff passes through 1; and by day 160 about 94 % of the population has had it.

Try: lower beta to 0.15 (R0 = 1.5) and watch the peak flatten and come later. Below R0 = 1 the infection dies out.

A room losing heat to 5 °C outside, with a time constant of two hours, and a heater that warms it at 10 °C an hour, switched by a thermostat with a dead band: on when the room falls through 19 °C, off when it rises through 21 °C. Between switches the room follows Newton's law of cooling. At each switch the right-hand side jumps, and the solver has to stop exactly there rather than step across it.

Too_cold and Too_warm are the two triggers. Each takes a snapshot of the time it fires (On_since, Off_since), and the heater is on while On_since is the later of the two: a memory of which way the room last crossed, made of two snapshots.

The switching times are known in closed form. Warming from 15 to 21 °C takes τ·ln(10/4) = 1.83 h; after that each cycle is τ·ln(16/14) = 0.27 h with the heater off and τ·ln(6/4) = 0.81 h with it on, 42 switches in the day. The run lands on every one of them to within half a millisecond.

Van der Pol's oscillator with μ = 1000, the standard stiff test problem. x creeps from 2 down towards 1 for most of each half-cycle and then jumps to −2 within a few milliseconds. The jumps come at about 807, 1614 and 2421 s, a period close to (3 − 2 ln 2)·μ ≈ 1614 s. During each jump y = dx/dt reaches ±1333 (4μ/3), and it is back near zero long before the next saved point, so on this chart y looks flat. Set the time spacing to "The solver's own points" to see the spikes, and how many steps the solver spends in them.

Long slow stretches and very fast transitions: that is stiffness. The NDF solver takes 1884 steps over the 3000 s. dp45 gets there too, but takes 1.7 million steps, about 900 times as many, because an explicit method's step is held down by stability, not accuracy, on the slow stretches as much as in the jumps.

Van der Pol's oscillator, x'' − μ(1 − x²)·x' + x = 0, as two compartments: x, and y = dx/dt. The damping is negative for small swings and positive for large ones, so every start except the origin winds onto the same closed orbit, a limit cycle of amplitude 2.009 and period 6.663. At μ = 1 the problem is not stiff, and dp45 crosses the twenty seconds in 185 steps. Both states go negative, so "cannot go negative" is off on each.

Try: start x at 0.1 instead of 2 and watch the swing grow onto the same cycle. Raise mu and the cycle sharpens into slow drifts and sudden jumps; the next example is this model at μ = 1000, the standard stiff test problem.
Canisters failing: a source term with barriers, and two disruptive events

4,500 spent-fuel canisters in a repository. None fails before year 1,000; after that the failures follow a Weibull with a characteristic life of 50,000 years and a shape of 2, the corrosion form. When a canister fails, 3% of its caesium and 0.5% of the rest is in the water at once (the instant release fraction) and the remainder waits for the fuel matrix, which dissolves at one part in ten million a year. The release goes into the near-field water, which is flushed to the geosphere; switch the mass-balance audit on under SIMULATION to watch the bookkeeping close. Two disruptive events act on it: an earthquake, a Poisson process at 2e-5 a year that fails 5% of the still-intact canisters at each occurrence, and a glaciation at 100,000 years that strips 80% of the biosphere out of the model. A deterministic run takes the earthquake in its expected-value form; a probabilistic run draws its occurrences — compare the staircase of Quake with its expected line.
No canister fails before this: the time the earliest corrosion process could breach one.
The Weibull scale: 63% of the canisters have failed one life after the first failure.
The fraction of the exposed fuel matrix dissolving per year. Everything bound in it leaves congruently.
Turnover of the near-field water: the fraction leaving for the geosphere per year.
Transit through the geosphere to the biosphere, as a first-order rate.
Earthquakes breaching canisters: one in fifty thousand years.
When the next ice sheet reaches the site.
The source term: the inventory starts inside the canisters and reaches the water only as they fail and the fuel dissolves. What leaves is the line drawn out of the block.
The water in and around the failed canisters. A solubility limit would go on the transfer out of here, as an availability.
What leaves the canisters. Its rate is the block itself, so there is nothing to set.
Dilution and dispersal out of the modelled biosphere.
An earthquake: at each occurrence 5% of the canisters still intact fail. Deterministically a hazard of 1e-6 a year on the intact inventory; in a probabilistic run, drawn occurrences.
The ice sheet arrives: 80% of what the biosphere holds is scraped away, out of the model.
